support.text: If you are thinking about suicide, or are worried about someone, free and confidential help is available. Find a helpline in your country, or in the US call or text 988.

capabilities.label: Capital
capabilities.desc: Money you can move: your own, or money you decide over.

capabilities.label: Build
capabilities.desc: Software, hardware, systems. You ship working things.

capabilities.label: Policy
capabilities.desc: You can get a rule changed: government, regulator, standards body.

capabilities.label: Distribute
capabilities.desc: You can put a message or a product in front of millions of people.

capabilities.label: Field
capabilities.desc: Logistics and operations in difficult places. You can be there.

capabilities.label: Convene
capabilities.desc: You can bring specific people together, and they will come.

causes.name: Household air pollution
causes.measure: deaths attributed to household air pollution

source.title: Household air pollution (fact sheet)
source.quote: responsible for an estimated 2.9 million deaths per year in 2021

causes.lever: Clean cooking. Around 2.1 billion people cook on open fires or inefficient stoves that burn kerosene, biomass or coal. Clean options exist: electricity, LPG, biogas, solar, and biomass stoves that meet WHO emission targets. What is short is affordable supply, and the finance and policy that put it into households.

causes.name: Lead exposure

source.title: Lead poisoning (fact sheet)
source.quote: Lead exposure was attributed to more than 3.5 million deaths globally in 2023

causes.lever: WHO describes the harm from lead as entirely preventable. The sources are known: mining, smelting, manufacturing and recycling, and lead in products such as paint, ceramic glazes and some traditional cosmetics. Most lead is used to make lead-acid batteries for vehicles. The work is measuring exposure, then regulating the sources and enforcing the limits.

causes.name: Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene
causes.measure: deaths from inadequate drinking-water, sanitation and hygiene

source.title: Sanitation (fact sheet)
source.quote: 1.4 million people die each year as a result of inadequate drinking-water, sanitation and hygiene

causes.lever: Most of these deaths are from diarrhoea, which WHO calls largely preventable with safe drinking-water, safely managed sanitation and handwashing. WHO describes the remaining task as government-led systems at scale, with financing, regulation and monitoring, instead of isolated projects. Treating water where it is collected, for example with chlorine dispensers, is one approach already in use.

causes.name: Road traffic crashes

source.title: Road traffic injuries (fact sheet)
source.quote: Approximately 1.16 million people die each year as a result of road traffic crashes

causes.lever: The measures are legal and physical: safe speeds, helmets, seat-belts and child restraints, roads designed for pedestrians and cyclists, and vehicle safety standards. WHO reports that correct helmet use cuts the risk of death in a crash by more than six times, and a seat-belt cuts it by up to half for vehicle occupants. These rules are set country by country and city by city.

causes.name: Deaths in pregnancy and childbirth
causes.measure: deaths of women during and after pregnancy and childbirth

source.title: Maternal mortality (fact sheet)
source.quote: About 260 000 women died during and following pregnancy and childbirth in 2023

causes.lever: WHO states that most of these deaths could have been prevented with skilled care before, during and after childbirth. Severe bleeding after birth is one of the main causes. A trial of more than 200 000 women, reported by WHO in 2023, found that measuring blood loss objectively and giving the recommended treatments together, instead of one after another, reduced severe bleeding by 60%. The gap is adoption of known protocols.

lever_source.title: WHO news release on the E-MOTIVE trial, 9 May 2023

causes.name: Drowning

source.title: Drowning (fact sheet)
source.quote: There are around 300 000 annual drowning deaths worldwide

causes.lever: Children under five account for nearly a quarter of drowning deaths. WHO's investment case finds two interventions cost-saving at scale: supervised day-care for pre-school children, and teaching school-age children basic swimming and water safety. Covering wells, doorway barriers and fencing around pools reduce exposure. All of it is field delivery.

orgs.name: Centre for Injury Prevention and Research, Bangladesh

causes.name: Snakebite envenoming

source.title: Snakebite envenoming (fact sheet)
source.quote: Around 81 410 to 137 880 people die each year because of snake bites

causes.lever: Effective treatment exists. WHO states that most deaths are preventable by making safe, effective antivenoms more widely available. Supply is the constraint: poor data on bites make need hard to estimate, and weak distribution and regulation have led manufacturers to cut production or raise prices. This is one of the few rows where manufacturing is the binding limit.

causes.name: Suicide

source.title: Suicide (fact sheet)
source.quote: More than 740 000 people die due to suicide every year

causes.lever: WHO treats suicide as a public health problem that can be prevented with timely, often low-cost interventions. Its LIVE LIFE approach names four: limiting access to the means, working with the media on responsible reporting, building life skills in adolescents, and early identification and follow-up of anyone affected. Each is a policy or service-delivery task.

causes.name: Tuberculosis

source.title: Tuberculosis (fact sheet)
source.quote: A total of 1.13 million people died from tuberculosis (TB) in 2025

causes.lever: TB is treated with antibiotics and can be fatal without them. WHO recommends rapid diagnostic tests as the first test for anyone with symptoms, and preventive treatment for people at high risk. The work is finding people who are ill, testing them quickly and supporting them through a full course of treatment.

causes.name: Malaria

source.title: Malaria (fact sheet)
source.quote: 282 million malaria cases and 610 000 malaria deaths in 80 countries

causes.lever: Malaria is preventable and curable. The core tools are insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying, preventive medicines given at the times of greatest risk, two vaccines WHO now recommends for children, and prompt treatment. The WHO African Region has 95% of the deaths, so the work is delivery there.

causes.name: HIV

source.title: HIV and AIDS (fact sheet)
source.quote: In 2025, an estimated 570 000 people died from HIV-related causes

causes.lever: HIV is preventable, and treatment makes it a manageable chronic condition: people on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load do not pass the virus to sexual partners. The levers are testing, uninterrupted access to treatment, and prevention options such as pre-exposure prophylaxis.

causes.name: Hepatitis B

source.title: Hepatitis B (fact sheet)
source.quote: In 2024, hepatitis B resulted in an estimated 1.1 million deaths

causes.lever: A safe vaccine, usually given soon after birth, offers nearly 100% protection. Infection in infancy becomes chronic in about 95% of cases, which is why vaccinating newborns matters most. For people already living with chronic infection, antiviral medicines exist. The work is vaccination at birth, testing and treatment.

causes.name: Hepatitis C

source.title: Hepatitis C (fact sheet)
source.quote: approximately 239 000 people died from hepatitis C

causes.lever: There is no vaccine, but antiviral medicines cure the infection. WHO recommends testing people at increased risk in every setting, and testing all adolescents and adults where more than 2% of the population has antibodies. Early detection and treatment prevent serious liver damage, so the work is testing and linking people to treatment.

causes.name: Rabies

source.title: Rabies (fact sheet)
source.quote: rabies causes 44 203 annual deaths

causes.lever: Dog bites and scratches cause 99% of human cases. Deaths are prevented in two ways: vaccinating dogs, and prompt treatment after a bite (wound washing, vaccine and, when indicated, immunoglobulin). WHO notes that these products are often inaccessible or unaffordable to the people who need them.

causes.name: Measles

source.title: Measles (fact sheet)
source.quote: there were an estimated 95 000 measles deaths globally

causes.lever: A safe and cost-effective vaccine exists. Most deaths are among unvaccinated or under-vaccinated children under five. WHO reports that 84% of children received a first dose in 2025, slightly below the 2019 level. The work is routine immunisation and campaigns that reach the children who are missed.

causes.name: Cervical cancer

source.title: Cervical cancer (fact sheet)
source.quote: around 604 000 new cases and around 280 000 deaths in 2024

causes.lever: Cervical cancer is largely preventable through HPV vaccination and screening, and curable when found early. The global targets are 90% of girls vaccinated by age 15, 70% of women screened by 35 and again by 45, and 90% of women with disease treated. Death rates are highest where these services are missing.

causes.name: Tobacco
causes.measure: deaths from tobacco, including second-hand smoke

source.title: Tobacco (fact sheet)
source.quote: Tobacco kills more than 7 million people each year

causes.lever: The measures are known and collected in WHO's MPOWER package. WHO calls tobacco taxes the most cost-effective way to reduce use, yet only 41 countries, covering 12% of the world's population, tax at the recommended level of at least 75% of the retail price. Advertising bans and pictorial health warnings are among the others. These are acts of legislation.

causes.name: Alcohol

source.title: Alcohol (fact sheet)
source.quote: around 2.6 million deaths were caused by alcohol consumption in 2019

causes.lever: WHO states that effective alcohol control interventions exist and should be used more; its SAFER initiative supports countries to put the high-impact, cost-effective ones in place. Access to treatment is very low: where data exist, no more than 14% of people with alcohol use disorders are in contact with treatment services.

causes.name: Outdoor air pollution
causes.measure: premature deaths caused by ambient (outdoor) air pollution

source.title: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution (fact sheet)
source.quote: estimated to have caused 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019

causes.lever: The sources are ones that policy controls: industry, transport, power generation and waste burning. WHO lists policies that have worked, including clean industrial technology, cleaner vehicles and fuels, urban transit, walking and cycling networks, and alternatives to the open burning of waste.

causes.name: Diarrhoeal disease in young children
causes.measure: deaths of children under 5 from diarrhoea

source.title: Diarrhoeal disease (fact sheet)
source.quote: Each year diarrhoea kills around 443 832 children under 5

causes.lever: WHO describes diarrhoeal disease as both preventable and treatable. Prevention is safe drinking-water, sanitation and handwashing with soap. Treatment is oral rehydration solution plus a 10 to 14 day course of zinc, which WHO reports shortens an episode by 25%. The work is getting these to the household when a child is sick.

causes.name: Pneumonia in young children
causes.measure: deaths of children under 5 from pneumonia

source.title: Pneumonia in children (fact sheet)
source.quote: killing 740 180 children in 2019

causes.lever: Pneumonia is the largest infectious cause of death in children. WHO says it can be prevented by immunisation, adequate nutrition and addressing environmental factors, and treated with amoxicillin, which trained community health workers can give with inexpensive oral antibiotics. The work is prevention and treatment that reach children early.

causes.name: Newborn deaths
causes.measure: deaths of newborns in their first 28 days

source.title: Newborn mortality (fact sheet)
source.quote: Globally 2.3 million children died in the first 28 days of life in 2022

causes.lever: The leading causes are premature birth, complications during birth, infections and congenital anomalies. Almost 80% of births now take place in health facilities, which WHO calls an opportunity to provide essential newborn care, yet few mothers and newborns stay the recommended 24 hours after birth. Quality of care around birth is the lever.

causes.name: Falls

source.title: Falls (fact sheet)
source.quote: approximately 842 000 deaths from falls worldwide

causes.lever: About 71% of fall deaths are among adults aged 60 and older. WHO lists the measures that work: exercise that challenges balance for older people, targeted reduction of hazards at home, child-safety measures, and fall-protection systems at work.

causes.name: Antimicrobial resistance
causes.measure: deaths associated with bacterial antimicrobial resistance

source.title: Antimicrobial resistance (fact sheet)
source.quote: associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021

causes.lever: WHO names the drivers: inappropriate use of antibiotics, poor infection prevention and control, and limited access to clean water, vaccines, diagnostics and medicines. The levers follow from them: stewardship of the antibiotics that still work, prevention of infections, and research and development of new medicines. The figure counts deaths associated with resistant infections, a wider measure than deaths caused by resistance alone.

orgs.name: Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership

causes.name: Cholera

source.title: Cholera (fact sheet)
source.quote: 21 000 to 143 000 deaths from cholera worldwide each year

causes.lever: Cholera can be fatal within hours if untreated, so quick access to treatment is crucial. Prevention is safe water, basic sanitation and hygiene; the oral cholera vaccine helps prevent and control outbreaks. WHO's approach combines surveillance, water and sanitation, access to treatment and vaccination campaigns.

orgs.name: Global Task Force on Cholera Control

causes.name: Typhoid fever

source.title: Typhoid (fact sheet)
source.quote: 110 000 people die from it every year

causes.lever: Typhoid is common where sanitation is poor and drinking water is unsafe. WHO lists safe water, adequate sanitation, hygiene among food handlers and vaccination as effective. Two typhoid conjugate vaccines prequalified by WHO since 2017 are being introduced into childhood immunisation programmes in endemic countries.

causes.name: Burns
causes.measure: deaths from exposure to fire, heat and hot substances

source.title: Burns (fact sheet)
source.quote: an estimated 163 000 people died worldwide from exposure to fire, heat and hot substances

causes.lever: WHO describes burns as preventable through safer products and environments, effective policy, and timely first aid and care. The risks it lists include open cooking fires and unstable stoves, hazardous fuels, unsafe gas and electrical installations, and limited access to first aid and medical care.

causes.name: Industrial trans fat
causes.measure: deaths attributed to intake of industrially produced trans fat

source.title: Trans fat (fact sheet)
source.quote: More than 278 000 deaths each year globally can be attributed to intake

causes.lever: WHO states that industrially produced trans fat can be eliminated and replaced with healthier fats or oils without changing the cost, taste or availability of food. Its REPLACE package supports governments to do this through regulatory limits. It is a task of legislation and reformulation with a defined end.

causes.name: Excess sodium
causes.measure: deaths associated with consuming too much sodium

source.title: Sodium reduction (fact sheet)
source.quote: 1.7 million deaths each year were associated with consuming too much sodium

causes.lever: Average adult intake is more than double the WHO recommendation. WHO calls sodium reduction one of the most cost-effective health measures, returning at least US$ 12 for every US$ 1 invested. Its recommended policies include reformulating foods to contain less sodium, with target levels, and mass media campaigns.

orgs.name: World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health

causes.name: Seasonal influenza

source.title: Influenza (seasonal) (fact sheet)
source.quote: It causes 290 000 to 650 000 respiratory deaths annually

causes.lever: WHO calls vaccination the best way to prevent the disease. Safe and effective vaccines have been used for more than 60 years, and yearly vaccination is recommended because immunity fades. WHO reports that 99% of deaths in children under five with influenza-related lower respiratory infections are in developing countries.

causes.name: Rheumatic heart disease

source.title: Rheumatic heart disease (fact sheet)
source.quote: claims approximately 360 000 lives each year

causes.lever: The disease starts as a streptococcal sore throat or skin infection, most often in childhood. It is prevented by treating those infections promptly with antibiotics and by improving living and housing standards. People who have had rheumatic fever need long-term antibiotic treatment to prevent further damage to the heart valves.

causes.name: Sickle-cell disease

source.title: Sickle-cell disease (fact sheet)
source.quote: 376 000 vs 34 400 deaths in 2021

causes.lever: Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly 80% of cases. WHO states that effective interventions exist, including early diagnosis through newborn screening, vaccinations to prevent infection and disease-modifying medicines such as hydroxyurea. The work is making them routine where most children with the disease are born.

causes.name: Asbestos at work
causes.measure: deaths caused by occupational exposure to asbestos

source.title: Asbestos (fact sheet)
source.quote: more than 200 000 deaths are estimated to be caused by occupational exposure to asbestos

causes.lever: WHO states that the most efficient way to prevent asbestos-related disease is to stop the use of all forms of asbestos, as more than 50 Member States have done by law, and to protect workers during maintenance where asbestos is already in place. It is a legislative decision followed by safe-removal practice.

causes.name: Extreme heat

source.title: Heat and health (fact sheet)
source.quote: approximately 489 000 heat-related deaths occur each year

causes.lever: WHO calls the health impacts of heat predictable and largely preventable. Deaths come on the same day and the days after extreme heat, so the response has to be fast: heat action plans, early warning systems and advisories, and emergency plans that map who is at risk.

causes.name: Unsafe food

source.title: Food safety (fact sheet)
source.quote: fall ill after eating contaminated food and 1.52 million die every year

causes.lever: WHO puts the first responsibility on governments: evidence-based policy, risk-based regulation and working food safety systems. For food handlers and households it publishes the Five keys to safer food. Children under five carry 29% of the health burden.
